http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/11/russi.text: Former United States Marine Robert Gilman is on his way back to the US after being freed from prison in Russia.US President Donald Trump said his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin had approved Gilman's release on humanitarian grounds. Gilman is said to be in poor health and was reportedly being held in a psychiatric ward of a hospital.Trump added that Moscow did not ask for a prisoner swap and that Gilman was set to land at Andrews Air Force Base near Washington, D.C on Tuesday evening."I just spoke to him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.Gilman was arrested and detained in Russia in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer following an incident on a train in Voronezh, to the south of Moscow. He was sentenced to four and a half years in prison over the incident, but his sentence was later extended to 10 years after he was alleged to have attacked prison staff.According to US Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Gilman was diagnosed with a "dissociative stupor" around 50 days ago and became "non-responsive.""He was essentially catatonic and also suffered a severe case of pneumonia," he said.In a post on X, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio thanked Russia for working with special envoy Steve Witkoff to secure Gilman's release, which he said would allow him "to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States."But Rubio made it clear that while Washington was grateful for the "positive step," the Trump administration would still be pushing for the "immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans.""The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home," he added.Gilman was one of a number of Americans detained in Russia. Others being held in the country include Stephen Hubbard, who the State Department has labelled a "wrongful detainee," and Army Staff Sergeant Gordon Black.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.text: Image source, Sonia Bellina's Instagram Image caption, Sonia Bellina had been visiting her family in southern France ahead of her 30th birthday By Malu Cursino Published 8 hours ago Two men have been detained after a young woman's burned body was found in a vineyard in southern France, the local prosecutor has said. In a statement on Wednesday, NÃ®mes prosecutor CÃ©cile Gensac confirmed the body found in the Saint-Gilles vineyard belonged to social media influencer Sonia Bellina. The 29-year-old had a following of around 260,000 on TikTok and was visiting her family in the area a month before her 30th birthday. The two men were taken into police custody on Wednesday due to "evidence suggesting their direct or indirect involvement in the incident", the prosecutor said. Police opened a murder investigation after a farmer found a body lying between rows of vines in the village near NÃ®mes on 12 August, but authorities did not confirm Bellina's identity for several days. The prosecutor's initial assessment was that the body belonged to a young woman, but more tests were needed to confirm who it was. In their latest update on Wednesday, Gensac said authorities could now confirm Bellina's identity after various investigations and DNA analysis. She acknowledged that Bellina's name had been "widely circulated over the past 48 hours". Prior to Gensac's update, the family's lawyer told French media that relatives were sure the body was Bellina's. Mourad Battikh told broadcaster RTL the 29-year-old's body had been "abandoned" and "almost thrown away like garbage" in what he described as "a murder of rare savagery". In the days since the scorched body was found, the identity and the circumstances of the death had sparked online speculation and rumours. A woman who described herself as the influencer's sister - but did not share her name - said she was convinced the body found in the Saint-Gilles vineyard was her sister's before it was confirmed. In an interview with the Midi Libre newspaper, she shared her family's ordeal and the harassment she says they have faced. According to her, some people have said Bellina "deserved what happened to her". The family's lawyer has been firm in regards to online comments, saying he would "let nothing slide". Anything published would be subject to scrutiny and reported if necessary, Battikh said. "The family is going through an extremely violent ordeal," he said in a press release, adding: "They request respect for their privacy and their grief and will not be making any further statements". https://deadline.com/print-article/12371.text: Musk, Misty Green and Fjord Bleecker Street/A24/Neon Festival favorites Musk , Misty Green and Fjord debut in limited release in a crowded indie market with awards season rolling along. Bleecker Street’s documentary by Oscar-winner Alex Gibney opens in four theaters in New York (Angelika and Lincoln Square, and LA (AMC Century City and Burbank). The buzzy portrait of Tesla, X and SpaceX chief Elon Musk premiered at Venice to critical acclaim, currently sitting at 100% on Rotten Tomatoes (off 28 reviews, see Deadline’s here ). The world’s richest person, MAGA donor, chainsaw waver, baby daddy and would-be Mars colonizer takes a thrashing. He didn’t participate in the doc and has trashed it on X but wanders across the frames as CGI avatar speaking words that Musk has spoken. Weekend Q&A screenings with Gibney were sold out in NYC and selling fast in Los Angeles, featuring producer and Pulitzer Prize-winner Ronan Farrow, journalist Zoe Schiffer, and former conservative influencer Ashley St. Clair, who shares a child with Musk and appears in the film. She refused to accept a financial settlement after her split with the multi-billionaire that would have required her to sign a non-disclosure agreement. The doc, which also screened at fests from TIFF to Zurich, Hamptons, Mill Valley Film Festival, Beyondfest and more, is a hefty 225 minutes long – plus a ten-minute intermission – which limits showtimes. Expands to about 300 screens next week. Musk has converged with Sony’s wide release this weekend of Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning , a sequel to The Social Network focused on the dangerous, sordid side of Facebook under founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg. And Luca Guadagnino’s Artificia l, a damning look at OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman isn’t coming out until December but has been making headlines since its world premiere at the New York Film Festival this week. Filmmakers clearly have big tech on their minds, especially AI, which is everywhere in the national conversation heading into the mid-term elections. Neon launches Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or-winning drama Fjord starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve at four theaters in NY and LA. A devout Romanian Norwegian couple named Gheorghius resettle in a village in a distant fjord where they become close to their neighbors, the Halbergs. Their children bond. When adolescent Elia Gheorghiu shows up at school with bruises, the community questions the traditional education the Gheorghiu children are getting from their parents. Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 91%. Deadline’s review here. The film reps the second Palme d’Or for Mungiu and the seventh consecutive win for Neon. The film also took the FIPRESCI Award at Cannes and is Romania’s Oscar entry for Best International Feature. A24 debuts Chris Rock’s Misty Green at six theaters across New York (Lincoln Square, Alamo, Union Square) and LA (Grove, Burbank, Century City). The TIFF-premiering original indie drama has a first-time lead in Rosalind Eleazar and sees Rock as a filmmaker returning to the director’s chair after more than a decade. Eleazar stars as a talented actress whose career has stalled fighting for a second act years after her Hollywood breakthrough. See Deadline review . Cohen Media Group is out with Winter Of The Crow starring Lesley Manville in 30+ markets and 63 screens, a mix of AMCs, Landmarks and arthouses. Manville’s U.K. professor Dr. Joan Andrews is invited to Warsaw to give a lecture in 1981 just as martial law is being imposed. As chaos engulfs the city, she witnesses a murder by the secret police and becomes a fugitive on the run fighting for her life and those of the students with whom she has allied. Directed and co-written by Kasia Adamik from a short story by Nobel and Booker Prize-winner Olga Tokarczuk. Premiered at TIFF 2025. Agnieszka Holland (Adamik’s mother) is an executive producer. At RT 94% off 16 reviews. Adventure drama The North from Picturehouse, written and directed by Bart Schrijver, opens at 17 locations including the Angelika and Empire in NYC and Laemmle’s Monica Film Center and Glendale in LA. Debut follows a preview early this week at 75 AMC Dolby cinemas. Stars Bart Harder and Carles Pulido as two friends in their early thirties – one Dutch, one Spanish – who reunite after a decade apart to hike Scotland’s grueling 330-mile West Highland Way and Cape Wrath Trail on a journey of unexpected self-discovery. https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymy.text: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has defended the leaders of Finland and Norway for reaching out to Russian leader Vladimir Putin as part of efforts to reach a peace deal. In a 90-minute call on Tuesday, Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre urged Putin to end his war on Ukraine. But some European leaders felt the call was a mistake, criticizing Stubb and Støre for undermining Europe’s unity in dealing with Russia’s president, who has been largely frozen out after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Advertisement Advertisement Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Zelenskyy praised the two Nordic leaders for their help, saying he had a “positive” view of them. “We really have very good relations with these countries. They truly help,” Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian leader said Putin had been taken out of diplomatic isolation last year when U.S. President Donald Trump met him in Alaska. “Since Alaska, Europeans have also been in contact with Russia,” Zelenskyy said. “They just haven’t done so as openly as the leaders of Norway and Finland.” Everyone understands that there have been contacts “at the national security adviser level and between intelligence agencies,” as well as talks that only emerged after they had happened, he said. “Here, though, everything is completely out in the open: discussions in advance, a full briefing, and transparent objectives. Finland and Norway are showing that they want to open another channel of communication, so that Europe can receive information not only through the United States and Russia can hear certain things directly,” Zelenskyy added. The question of whether — and how — Europe should talk to Putin is a sore subject for officials and diplomats among Ukraine’s allies in the EU and beyond. On Tuesday, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very skeptical” about the Finnish-Norwegian joint call and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement” of Russia. Advertisement Advertisement One official from a national capital, granted anonymity like others to speak candidly about sensitive issues, said formats like the E3 (Germany, France and the U.K.) worked well. Fracturing the unified European voice by letting each country start its own talks with Moscow would be a bad thing, the official added. The Italian government was irked by Stubb and Støre’s call with Putin, with officials saying it exposed Europe’s failure to agree who should represent the region in peace talks. A government official from Rome warned that separate national initiatives and constantly shifting diplomatic formats risk further eroding influence, saying Europe “cannot continue to act randomly and in formats that change from week to week.” Rome wants the urgent appointment of representatives with a shared European mandate to defend the continent’s interests and security. “The negotiations will not wait,” the official said. The reaction from the Brussels institutions to the Norway-Finland initiative has been muted so far, while hinting at the sensitivity of the subject. “We take note of the call, which took place solely on a bilateral basis,” said Paula Pinho, spokesperson for the European Commission. “These negotiations are happening in different formats, different places and different levels involving heads of states and government, ministers, senior diplomats and officials. The EU is involved.”
